Cinematic wide establishing shot of a peaceful urban park at golden hour, shot on a full-frame
sensor with a 28mm spherical prime at roughly T2.8, camera locked off at eye level approximately
1.5 meters above the ground, dead-level horizon, no tilt, no dutch. The lens sits directly over a
broad pale-stone walking path that begins wide in the immediate foreground and curves gently right
to left into the middle distance, leading the eye toward a small circular tiered stone fountain
about forty meters away. The path is laid in large rectangular limestone pavers, warm bone-grey,
with fine darker mortar joints, subtle foot-polish sheen on the raised centers, faint damp patches
near the pond edge, and a few scattered dry leaves pressed flat against the stone.
A calm ornamental pond fills the lower-left foreground, its still surface holding a mirrored,
slightly darkened inversion of the tree canopy and a long stretched specular reflection of the low
sun. A thin ribbon of glowing ground mist hovers ten to twenty centimeters above the water and
drifts across the near lawn edge, catching the backlight and separating the foreground from the
midground. The pond is rimmed with weathered stone coping and a soft fringe of tall reeds and
grasses along its far bank.
Dense mature deciduous trees — broad plane and oak canopies — frame the composition on three sides.
Heavy dark branches sweep across the top of the frame in silhouette, their leaves rimmed with hot
gold where the sun passes through. One massive tree trunk dominates the right foreground, deeply
textured with fissured bark, moss in the shaded grooves, and warm raking light catching the ridges
along its left side. Shafts of low sunlight break through the canopy and fall in soft elongated
patches across the lawn and path. The lawn is neatly maintained, evenly mown with faint mower
stripes, deep green in shadow and translucent yellow-green where the sun grazes it.
Beyond the fountain, past the green canopy, a softly hazy city skyline rises — glass and concrete
towers rendered in low contrast, desaturated blue-grey, their upper edges catching pale gold,
progressively dissolving into atmospheric haze with distance. Strong aerial perspective: crisp
detail in the foreground bark and stone, gentle falloff through the midground trees, near-silhouette
softness at the skyline.
On the right side of the path, beneath the large tree, sits exactly one empty park bench: dark green
painted wooden slats, three across the seat and three across the back, mounted on black wrought-iron
end frames with a simple scrolled Victorian profile. The paint shows honest age — micro-chipping at
the slat edges, slight sun-fade on the upward faces, faint rust bloom at the iron feet where they
meet the paving. The bench faces the path and pond, angled slightly toward camera, fully unoccupied,
nothing resting on it.
Immediately beside the bench, near its outer edge on the side away from camera, stands exactly one
small cylindrical public dustbin: brushed stainless steel, roughly waist height, with a plain domed
lid, a single rectangular side opening, and vertical brushed grain catching a soft vertical highlight
from the low sun. It sits flush and naturally on the paving with a grounded contact shadow. One bench,
one bin, nothing else.
Lighting: late-afternoon backlight with the sun low, roughly eight degrees above the horizon, just
outside the frame behind the tree line at upper center-left. Warm 3200-3600K key raking through the
foliage, cool ambient bounce filling the shadows, gentle organic halation around the brightest leaf
edges and the water specular, no hard artificial lens flares or streaks. Deep green shadows retaining
detail rather than crushing to black.
Style: photoreal cinematic still, subdued filmic color grade with lifted milky blacks, restrained
saturation, warm golden highlights rolling off gently, slight teal push in the shade. Natural depth
with a mild focus falloff — foreground bark and paving sharp, fountain softening slightly, skyline
softest. Fine natural film grain. 16:9 widescreen, 2.0 aspect-safe framing, high dynamic range,
extremely high detail.

At the hollow's mouth a BROWN scribble begins — a loose patch — and grows drawing by drawing into a big pear shape; the black outline is drawn around it in one travelling line: up the back, over the rounded rump, round the breast, up the long NECK to the small head, the long bill drawn as a wedge pointing left; the fill scribbled in — tan, brown, dark umber — rows of brown U-marks flicked across the back; the LEFT WING drawn lowered like a blanket in front of her breast with the royal-blue rectangle pressed in and a white line beside it; two orange leg strokes and big three-toed feet; the dark crown and eye-stripe drawn; and LAST her EYE — one black-brown dot pressed hard with a white gap left — and she is looking down at the empty place under her wing. The picture is redrawn a little larger over these seconds — a slow drawn push toward her.

BEAT 4 (0:13–0:16) — TYANPA IS DRAWN. Under the edge of her wing, at the lower-left of her breast, a small YELLOW scribble blooms — a round head — the black outline drawn round it; the grey-brown crown patch scribbled on top; the single dark SPOT drawn beside the eye on the viewer's left; the small grey wedge bill; yellow ticks flicked round the head; the top of his yellow body scribbled below the head where it shows past the wing; and LAST his EYE — a black dot pressed hard with a white gap — open, looking up at her. THE RUN — ANIMATION PRINCIPLES WRITTEN INTO THE BODY, energy 100%, about 4 strides per second, left to right across frame:
- ANTICIPATION: before every push-off the body dips — knees fold, chest drops a fraction toward the grass, the head lowers a hair — for two frames, then the push.
- PUSH-OFF AND STRETCH: the planted leg drives straight back, toes spreading then pointing; the body lifts and STRETCHES long — neck extending, spine lengthening, tail trailing — the body slightly taller-and-thinner than at rest at the moment of highest speed.
- THE FLOAT: at the top of each bound BOTH FEET ARE OFF THE GROUND — trailing leg straight back, leading leg tucked up under the belly with toes curled — held for a beat; the body relaxes to its normal shape at the apex; the path of his head through the air is a smooth ARC, never a straight line.
- LANDING AND SQUASH: the leading foot slaps flat onto the grass, the leg folds to take the weight, the body COMPRESSES — shorter and wider for one frame after contact, the belly down nearly brushing the grass tips, the down on his chest and flanks bouncing outward — then the next anticipation dip flows straight into the next push.
- TIMING AND SPACING: fast out of the ground, slowing into the top of the arc, hanging, then accelerating down into the landing; the spacing of his body positions is tight near the ground and open at the apex.
- FOLLOW-THROUGH AND OVERLAP: the HEAD lags the body by a frame — bobbing forward-and-back once per stride, dipping as the body lands and lifting as it rises, the neck absorbing the shock; the WINGS are held up and back for balance and beat once per stride, arriving late behind the body's motion, one always higher than the other, overshooting and settling; the TAIL flicks up on the push and drops a frame after the landing; the DOWN on his flanks and rump ripples backward and settles a beat after every landing; the crown feathers flatten with speed and lift at the apex.
- EXAGGERATION WITHIN WEIGHT: everything a fraction larger than a real duckling would do — the stretch, the squash, the float, the head bob — but never beyond what his small heavy body could physically do; feet always drive the motion, nothing floats without a push.
- Head turned UP and slightly toward the butterflies streaming over him, bill open, eye wide and bright, gaze following one butterfly then another. Every landing kicks grass, petals and grit back in a small arc. A straight line, no weaving.

THE BUTTERFLY PHYSICS — FOOTFALL-TRIGGERED, EACH ONE ITS OWN:
- THE TRIGGER: only a FOOTFALL lifts them. Half a beat after each foot strikes, the butterflies resting within about a hand's width of that foot — on the shore grass, the flower heads, the pebbles — leave the ground. Everything further than that stays resting. Everything ahead of him stays resting until his foot arrives. His slipstream may tug the ones already airborne, but it lifts nothing new.
- THE CHAOS: each burst is a handful of butterflies and EACH ONE FLIES DIFFERENTLY — one shoots straight up two duckling-heights; one skims sideways just above the flowers; one flips over twice and drops back onto a flower; one loops back the way he came; one climbs slowly in a wobbling spiral; one flutters hard and gets nowhere; one glides flat and fast to the left; one tumbles end over end in the grit he kicked up; one lands on his back for a stride and lifts off again. Different speeds — from barely moving to darting. Different heights — from grass-tip to high above him. Different directions — every point of the compass. Different wing rates. Nothing repeats. Two butterflies never fly in parallel.
- THE TRAIL: because he strides five times a second, the bursts overlap into a low ragged trail of airborne butterflies behind him along the shore — thickest right behind his feet, thinning back to the left where the earliest ones have already re-landed — but the trail is made of individuals, each visibly on its own path, never a flowing ribbon. It rises no higher than about four times his height. Ahead of him: nothing in the air.
- THE SETTLE: three or four duckling-lengths behind him the disturbed butterflies are drifting down and re-landing, each in its own time and place.
- THE REFLECTION: the whole thing — him, the bursts, the ragged trail — is mirrored in the still lake below.

HEAD CLOSE-UP PANEL: the tan head in short strokes going different directions; a dark umber crown as a heavy band across the top, its lower edge ragged; the eye-stripe a thick dark stroke through the eye that runs a little too far back; the eye a black-brown dot pressed hard with a small white gap left in it, slightly too large and a touch too far forward; a pale stroke above the stripe that only goes halfway; the bill a long orange wedge coloured in two tones with the dark umber dots on top drawn too big and too few, a black dot nostril, a straight dark line for the mouth, a dark grey scribble at the tip; the neck below in flecked tan strokes that stop abruptly at the cut edge. Real materials: real wax crayon with visible build-up and pressure changes, white paper grain through the colour, a few crayon crumbs on the grey backdrop, the wax shining faintly under the lamp. CONSISTENCY: the same duck, the same crayon colours, the same boy's hand and the same cut-out method in all four panels — the same paper, crayon set and lamp as the Tyanpa sheet. TECHNICAL: seamless neutral mid-grey paper backdrop, soft diffused even lamp light from the upper left with one soft real shadow per cutout, true-to-life crayon colour, photographed straight down with a full-frame 85mm lens look, sharp focus on the paper grain and wax. This is a photograph of a real twelve-year-old's crayon drawings cut out and laid on grey paper — not a digital painting, not a filter, not vector, not 3D, not neat, not professional. Real mallard duckling anatomy — dry fluffy down with every filament resolved, small dark bill, dark eye-stripe, tiny orange feet, one wet living eye with a catch-light. COMPOSITION — LOW ANGLE, LOOKING UP INTO A SKY FULL OF BUTTERFLIES:
- The camera is DOWN at the level of the grass tips, tilted UP about 30 degrees, so the frame is almost all SKY. The ground appears only as a thin ragged band along the very bottom edge — grass tips, flower heads and a few taller stems in silhouette-and-light — no horizon line visible, no distant landscape, no mountains, no trees on a horizon.
- <<<5acf4096-02e3-4006-ab1e-b27aafcc9151>>> (butter-yellow mallard duckling, dry and fluffy, small dark bill, dark eye-stripe, tiny orange feet) is LEFT OF CENTRE, rising out of the bottom of frame so that his body from the breast up is in frame and his legs disappear into the grass band. He is RUNNING from left to right in a THREE-QUARTER FRONT view — his breast and the near side of his body toward the camera, seen from below so his chest and the underside of his chin loom. THE RUN, energy 100%, as a pose: caught at the top of a bound, body pitched forward and stretched, both wing stubs flung UP and BACK, the near one higher, down streaming off their tips, the near leg driving back out of frame; and his HEAD TURNED UP and toward the RIGHT, neck stretched, crown tilted back, bill open wide in a shout of joy, his eye wide and bright, looking UP into the butterflies streaming over him — he runs looking at them, not where he is going. Every butterfly lit from the upper left — the near ones bright and translucent, wings glowing with colour, the far ones sparkling as they catch the sun; the clouds brilliant white on their sun-side, soft grey beneath. Mild lens flare from the upper-left corner. Open shadows, nothing black; the grass band at the bottom warm and back-lit.

ACTION — 12 seconds: black, the eyelids fight, the world resolves, the scream, the flight.
BEAT 1 (0:00–0:01.5) — BLACK. Full black frame. Sound only: quick shallow sniffing pulses very close, a whisker brushing something, a drip, distant river.
BEAT 2 (0:01.5–0:02.5) — FIRST CRACK. A thin horizontal slit of light opens across the middle of the black — soft dark eyelid edges above and below, blurred, trembling — and through it a formless smear: a soft pink blob, a few pale streaks that will become whiskers, violet light behind. The slit holds a quarter second, sags, and closes to black. Slow-in on the opening, slow-out on the close.
BEAT 3 (0:02.5–0:04.0) — SECOND ATTEMPT. The lids part again, wider this time, shuddering — the image doubled and swimming, heavily out of focus, the pink blob now clearly a nose too close to see, the whisker-streaks sweeping across the frame as huge soft white lines, the vole's head a warm-dappled brown mass above it, the canted ground and trunks behind it a wash of blue-violet with no edges. The nose twitches in the blur — it is still sniffing, it has not moved. The lids sag to half, catch, hold — she is fighting them.
BEAT 4 (0:04.0–0:06.0) — THE WORLD RESOLVES. The lids lift fully and stay. Over two seconds the image pulls itself together — cinematic, not mechanical: the double image slides into one, the swim stops, contrast and colour deepen from a milky wash into real dusk light, and focus travels inward from the far trunks, across the silt, across the whiskers, and lands last and hardest on the vole: its wet pink nose a centimetre from the lens, nostrils pulsing, the muzzle fur crisp, two black eyes above it catching the last light, the buff spot behind its LEFT eye, the gold gobo on its crown. Fully sharp at 0:06.0.
BEAT 5 (0:06.0–0:06.4) — THE BREATH BEFORE. Absolute stillness for a third of a second. The vole's nose stops mid-sniff. Its whiskers hold. Both black eyes on the lens. Nothing moves. Silence.
BEAT 6 (0:06.4–0:07.3) — THE SCREAM AND THE JOLT. THE CAMERA IS HER HEAD SNAPPING UP: a violent rise of about 30 cm with a hard roll from the ~55-degree cant to nearly level — the world whips, the ground drops out of the bottom of frame, trunks and sky smear in heavy motion blur, a half-frame black eyelid flash at the peak — an OVERSHOOT past level, a quick settle, then a residual sway, the unsteady neck of an animal unconscious a moment ago. On the rise a loud, sharp, startled quack — one harsh burst. In the same instant THE VOLE IS TERRIFIED: anticipation first — three frames of compression, body squeezing down onto the silt, whiskers snapping flat back along the head, eyes wide and fixed on the thing rising over it — then the explosive retreat: it does NOT turn first, it SCRAMBLES BACKWARD, hind legs shoving, belly scraping the ground, forepaws paddling, two body-lengths in reverse with mud flicking, its whole body flattened and small.
BEAT 7 (0:07.3–0:09.5) — THE FLIGHT. SUBJECT — @char_mother_duck (matches input 100% — female mallard, plumage soaked and slicked dark, dark crown stripe and eye-stripe, blue-white speculum, pale-grey and olive bill, orange legs) lying senseless on her side exactly as in @sensless_ducks, head on its cheek, both eyes closed, wing fallen open; @char_3-ducklings (matches input 100% — EXACTLY THREE butter-yellow ducklings, drenched and spiky) senseless at her breast under the wing; @char_vole (matches input 100% — chestnut-brown European water vole, blunt rounded muzzle, dark-pink nose, small black wide-set eyes, pale buff spot behind the LEFT eye, paler RIGHT forepaw, small ears hidden in fur, long white whiskers, furred tail; here fur damp and slicked into spikes, mud on paws and muzzle, body about 19 cm — small beside the duck, normal size). Goal + beat: total stillness, then a small harmless life enters and comes to sniff at a sleeper who does not wake — her eyes stay closed to the last frame; the vole's curiosity against her stillness is the emotional payload. Animal performance capture: real waterfowl and real rodent micro-mechanics only, nothing anthropomorphic, nothing cartooned. WB 4300K. ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, no cuts.

LOCATION — @sensless_ducks is the START FRAME and STYLE REFERENCE: the flood-wrecked birch riverbank at late evening — fallen silver birch trunk behind her, wet dark silt and pebbles, the puddle at her bill, hanging leafy branches, dark defocused flood debris in the foreground corners, muted violet-rose dusk sky in the tree gaps, no sun in frame, soft-edged dappled gobo light gathered on her head, cool blue-violet dusk shadow everywhere else, thin low mist. The camera creeps but the world stays exactly this.

ACTION — 13 seconds: stillness, arrival, sniff, and she does not wake.
BEAT 1 (0:00–0:04) — STILLNESS. Nothing moves but breath: her chest lifts once, slow and shallow, and settles; one duckling's flank rises with a tiny faster breath; a single drop falls from the branch above into the puddle and the ring spreads to her bill. The gobo patches on her head shift almost imperceptibly as leaves stir. No other motion.
BEAT 2 (0:04–0:08) — THE VOLE ENTERS. From the RIGHT edge of frame, low along the ground line at the height of her head, @char_vole enters nose-down, foraging: a short quick scurry of about three body-lengths — back hunched, belly almost brushing the silt, nose pushing through wet leaf litter, tail dragging and trailing a half-beat behind the body — then a FREEZE, whole body still, only the whiskers sweeping forward and the nose twitching; a second shorter scurry; a second freeze, and here it RISES onto its hind legs for one beat, forepaws tucked, nose lifted, whiskers fanned, scenting the air toward her — anticipation — then drops and comes on in a third scurry that stops about a bill-length from her face. The ducks do not move.
BEAT 3 (0:08–0:11) — THE SNIFF. The vole steps in, slow now, RIGHT forepaw first, and brings its nose to within two centimetres of her cheek feathers: quick shallow sniffing pulses, the nose and whiskers twitching, whisker tips brushing the wet feathers beside her closed eye; it cocks its head a few degrees, sniffs along her bill toward the puddle, comes back to the eye. Its body stays low and hunched, weight forward on the forepaws, tail still on the ground behind it. No sound from it but tiny claws on wet pebbles.
BEAT 4 (0:11–0:13) — SHE DOES NOT WAKE. The vole's nose stays at her face, sniffing, whiskers brushing the closed lid; it cocks its head the other way, a few degrees, and holds — waiting. Her eye stays shut, the lid smooth and still, no flicker, no tremble. Her only movement is one slower, deeper breath that lifts her chest and settles, the bill parting a fraction on the exhale and closing again. Nothing else on her moves — neck slack, wing open, ducklings still. END on her closed eye in the gold dapple and the vole's twitching nose almost touching it, camera still creeping in.

A SUBTLE DOLLY-IN throughout — a slow creeping push toward her head over the full 13 seconds; in BEAT 1 give it a faint dolly-zoom quality, the lens widening a touch as the camera pushes, so the background trunk and sky stretch back very slightly while her head holds its size — a quiet unease; from BEAT 2 the push continues as a plain slow dolly-in with no further focal change. Focus locked on her closed eye the entire take; when the vole arrives it enters the same focal plane and both are sharp, the ducklings a touch soft, trunk and sky softer, foreground debris the softest. Her eye is the compositional anchor on the right third; the vole travels along the bottom-right toward it and stops just short of the frame's focal point so nothing ever covers her eye. No handheld shake, no cuts, no zoom after BEAT 1, no slow motion.
